Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 103, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2):

﴿By time﴾ [1] ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [2] ﴿Except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised one another to truth and advised one another to patience﴾ [3].

God Most High swears by al-'Asr (time/the afternoon), an oath intended to emphasize the report, as is the custom of the Qur'anic oaths.

The sworn-by thing is among the manifestations of the wondrous creation of the Lord, indicating His great power and the breadth of His knowledge.

Al-'Asr has meanings, and the intended one must be something that is no more than a state indicating an attribute of the divine acts. It is specified either by its being attached to something that is estimated (to be understood), or by context, or by prior reference. Whatever is intended by it here, the oath by it, insofar as it is a time, reminds of the great power of God Most High in creating the world and its conditions, and of great blessed matters, such as the specific prayer, or a particular blessed period.

The most common usage of the word 'asr is that it is a proper noun by predominance for a certain time, between the end of the time of Dhuhr and the yellowing of the sun (iṣfirar al-shams), so its beginning is when the shadow of an object becomes equal to it after the measure it had at the sun's zenith, and it extends until the shadow of an object becomes twice its measure after the shadow it had at the sun's zenith. That is the time of the sun's yellowing, and 'asr is the beginning of the evening (al-'ashi). It is followed by al-asil and reddening (al-ihmirar), which is before the sunset. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"She was startled by a sound, and the hunter frightened her at 'asr, when the evening had drawn near."

That time signals the approaching end of the day, and reminds of the creation of the sun and the earth, and the system of the earth's movement around the sun, which is the movement from which night and day are formed every day. In this respect it is like the oath by the forenoon, by the night and the day, and by the dawn, among the atmospheric conditions that change with the change of the direction of the sun's rays toward the terrestrial sphere.

At that time people prepare to cease their work of the day, such as tending their fields and gardens, and their trades in their markets. It thus reminds of the wisdom of the system of human society and what God inspired in human nature of habit in work and order for its beginning and its cessation. In it people hasten to return to their homes to spend the night and to be at ease with their families and children. It is of the blessing or of the bliss, and in it there is an allusion to reminding of a life like this when people's terms draw near after passing through the stages of youth, middle age, and old age.

Its definiteness with the article, on these aspects, is the definiteness of mental reference (al-'ahd al-dhihni), i.e., every 'asr.

Al-'Asr is also applied to the prayer timed to the time of 'Asr, and it is a greatly esteemed prayer. It has been said that it is what is meant by "the middle" in His saying: ﴿Guard over the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. And there came in a hadith: ("Whoever misses the 'Asr prayer, it is as if he has been robbed of his family and his property"). And there occurs in the authentic hadith: ("Three whom God will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection") — and he mentioned: "and a man who swore a false oath after 'Asr over a commodity, for which he was given what he was not given." Its definiteness on this view is the definiteness of reference, and it became a proper noun by predominance, as is the case with many generic nouns defined by the article, like al-'aqaba.

Al-'Asr is also applied to a known period for the existence of a generation of people, or a king, or a prophet, or a religion, and it is specified by annexation, so one says: 'asr al-Fitahl, 'asr Ibrahim, 'asr al-Iskandar, 'asr al-jahiliyya. It is permissible that this sense is intended here, and that what is meant is the era of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the definiteness in it is the definiteness of presential reference, like the definiteness in "the day" in your saying: "I did such-and-such today." So the oath by it is like the oath by his life in His saying: (By your life). Al-Fakhr said: "He, Exalted, swore by His time in this verse, and by His place in His saying: ﴿And you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], and by his life in His saying: (By your life)." End of quote.

It is also permissible that the era of Islam in its entirety is intended, which is the final of the eras of religions for this world. The Prophet (ﷺ) likened the era of the Islamic community, relative to the era of the Jews and the era of the Christians, to the period after the 'Asr prayer until sunset, in his saying: "The likeness of the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians is like a man who hired workers to work for him until night. The Jews worked until midday, then said: 'We have no need of your wage, and what we did is void.' He hired others after them and said: 'Complete the rest of your day, and you will have what I stipulated for them.' They worked until the time of the 'Asr prayer, then said: 'What we did is void for you, and you will have the wage that you set for us.' He hired a people to work the rest of their day, and they worked until the sun set and completed the wage of both groups. You are they." So perhaps that prophetic parable has a connection with the allusion to the era of Islam in this verse.

It is also permissible that 'asr in this verse be interpreted as the whole time. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about al-'Asr, and he said: 'Your Lord swore by the end of the day.'" These meanings are not covered in their possibility by any word other than the word 'asr.

The relevance of the oath by al-'Asr to the purpose of the surah, on the intention of the era of Islam, is evident, for it clarifies the condition of people in the era of Islam, between those who disbelieved in it and those who believed and fulfilled their share of the deeds that Islam brought, and it makes known the condition of those who embraced Islam and whose deeds had varying shortcoming. As for the conditions of the nations that were before Islam, they varied according to the coming of messengers to some nations, and the remaining of some nations without laws, adhering to other than the religion of Islam, such as polytheism, or to a religion whose abrogation Islam brought, such as Judaism and Christianity. God Most High said: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and he in the Hereafter will be among the losers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85], in the surah of Al 'Imran.

The definiteness of "al-insan" (mankind) is the definiteness of the genus, meant to be comprehensive, and it is a customary comprehensiveness, because it encompasses the individuals of the human species existing at the time of the revelation of the verse, which is the time of the appearance of Islam, as you have learned shortly. It is specified for the people to whom the call reached in the lands of the world, with its variation. When the exception was made from it of those who believed and did righteous deeds, the ruling remained established for those other than the believers, as will come.

Al-khusr (loss) is a verbal noun, and it is the opposite of profit in trade. It is borrowed here for bad outcome for one who thinks a good outcome is for himself, and that is the lasting outcome, which is the outcome of man in his Hereafter, of bliss or punishment.

It was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿So their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] in surah al-Baqarah. And its counterparts recur in the Qur'an, near and far.

The adverbial form (zarfiyya) in His saying: ﴿indeed, in loss﴾ is figurative: it likened the constant attachment of loss to the encompassing of the container by the contained, so it was more eloquent than saying: "Indeed, man is a loser."

The coming of this report in generality, with its emphasis by the oath and the emphatic particle in its answer, conveys awe and warning regarding the condition that encompasses most people.

It was followed by the exception in His saying: ﴿except those who have believed﴾ and so on. Thus the ruling becomes fully established in the hearer's mind, clarifying that people are of two groups: a group to whom loss reaches, and a group to whom none of it reaches. Those who believed and did righteous deeds, loss does not reach them in any way, provided they do not leave any of the righteous deeds by committing their opposites, which are the evil deeds.

Among the greatest righteous deeds is repentance from sins for those who commit them. Whoever has the attribute of faith realized in him and did not do evil deeds, or did them and repented of them, then the opposite of loss is realized for him, which is figurative profit, that is, the goodness of the outcome of his affair. As for whoever did not do righteous deeds and did not repent of his evil deeds, the ruling of the excepted-from is realized in him, which is loss.

This loss varies. The greatest and most enduring of it is the loss resulting from the absence of faith in God's oneness and the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). Beyond that, the degrees of loss vary according to the abundance of evil deeds, outward and inward. And what Islam has set as degrees of deeds

[continued in next part]

[Page 534]

The Almighty's saying ﴿and they enjoined one another to the truth, and they enjoined one another to patience﴾ encompasses the establishing of all the religious interests. Thus the Islamic creeds and the religious ethics are included in the truth, and righteous deeds and avoiding evil deeds are included in patience.

Cultivating patience is the foundation of all the virtues of character, for training oneself in praiseworthy character necessarily involves a person compelling himself to oppose many desires. Opposing them involves hardship, which requires patience in bearing it, until noble character becomes a settled disposition (malakah) for the one who has trained his soul in it. As 'Amr ibn al-'As said:

*"When a man does not leave a food he loves,*
*and does not restrain a deluded heart wherever it wanders,*
*he will soon find for himself, through all time, a disgrace,*
*whose like, when mentioned, fills the mouths."*

[Page 534 continued]

Likewise, all righteous deeds involve compelling the soul to abandon what it inclines toward. In a hadith: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires." And from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Patience is a mount that does not stumble."

The discussion of patience has already been treated at length at the Almighty's saying ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:45] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The form of the verb "enjoining one another" with the truth and with patience indicates that the condition of believers' lives is to be founded on the widespread mutual exhortation to these two as a constant habit. This requires that believers be characterized by upholding the truth and by patience with what is disliked in the interests of Islam and its community. This accords with the customary understanding of people: no one enjoins another to constantly maintain a matter unless he himself regards that matter as deserving of constancy, since it is rare for anyone to undertake a matter of truth that he does not himself practice, or to urge patience while being impatient himself. The Almighty has said, rebuking the Children of Israel: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book? Will you not reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:44]. This meaning was also mentioned earlier at the Almighty's saying ﴿and do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾ [al-Fajr 89:18] in Surah al-Fajr.

Surah al-Humazah

This surah is named in the mushaf and in most tafsir works "Surat al-Humazah" with the definite article. In Sahih al-Bukhari and some tafsir works it is titled "Surat Wayl li-kulli humazah." Al-Fayruzabadi, in Basa'ir dhawi al-tamyiz, mentions that it is also called "Surat al-Hutamah" because this word occurs in it.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the thirty-second in the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Qiyamah and before Surat al-Mursalat.

Its verses number nine by consensus.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning a group of polytheists who had set themselves up to revile and insult the Muslims and to fabricate evil reports about them. Among these polytheists named were al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Jamil ibn Ma'mar of Banu Jumah (this man embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest and was present at Hunayn), and al-'As ibn Wa'il of Banu Sahm. All of them were among the chiefs of Quraysh. Also named were al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth and al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafiyyan, chiefs of the Thaqif from the people of al-Ta'if. All of these were people of wealth in the pre-Islamic period, flourishing through their riches and nobility. The verses of the surah came in general terms, so its ruling encompassed those named and whoever was of their kind among the polytheists, and their names were not mentioned.

* * *

The purpose of this surah is a warning to a group of polytheists who made defaming and slandering the Muslims a form of harm to them, hoping that the weariness of these kinds of harm would drive them to turn away from Islam and return to polytheism.

Al-'Asr is also applied to a known period for the existence of a generation of people, or a king, or a prophet, or a religion, and it is specified by annexation, so one says: 'asr al-Fitahl, 'asr Ibrahim, 'asr al-Iskandar, 'asr al-jahiliyya. It is permissible that this sense is intended here, and that what is meant is the era of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the definiteness in it is the definiteness of presential reference, like the definiteness in "the day" in your saying: "I did such-and-such today." So the oath by it is like the oath by his life in His saying: (By your life). Al-Fakhr said: "He, Exalted, swore by His time in this verse, and by His place in His saying: ﴿And you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], and by his life in His saying: (By your life)." End of quote.

It is also permissible that the era of Islam in its entirety is intended, which is the final of the eras of religions for this world. The Prophet (ﷺ) likened the era of the Islamic community, relative to the era of the Jews and the era of the Christians, to the period after the 'Asr prayer until sunset, in his saying: "The likeness of the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians is like a man who hired workers to work for him until night. The Jews worked until midday, then said: 'We have no need of your wage, and what we did is void.' He hired others after them and said: 'Complete the rest of your day, and you will have what I stipulated for them.' They worked until the time of the 'Asr prayer, then said: 'What we did is void for you, and you will have the wage that you set for us.' He hired a people to work the rest of their day, and they worked until the sun set and completed the wage of both groups. You are they." So perhaps that prophetic parable has a connection with the allusion to the era of Islam in this verse.

It is also permissible that 'asr in this verse be interpreted as the whole time. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about al-'Asr, and he said: 'Your Lord swore by the end of the day.'" These meanings are not covered in their possibility by any word other than the word 'asr.

The relevance of the oath by al-'Asr to the purpose of the surah, on the intention of the era of Islam, is evident, for it clarifies the condition of people in the era of Islam, between those who disbelieved in it and those who believed and fulfilled their share of the deeds that Islam brought, and it makes known the condition of those who embraced Islam and whose deeds had varying shortcoming. As for the conditions of the nations that were before Islam, they varied according to the coming of messengers to some nations, and the remaining of some nations without laws, adhering to other than the religion of Islam, such as polytheism, or to a religion whose abrogation Islam brought, such as Judaism and Christianity. God Most High said: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and he in the Hereafter will be among the losers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85], in the surah of Al 'Imran.

The definiteness of "al-insan" (mankind) is the definiteness of the genus, meant to be comprehensive, and it is a customary comprehensiveness, because it encompasses the individuals of the human species existing at the time of the revelation of the verse, which is the time of the appearance of Islam, as you have learned shortly. It is specified for the people to whom the call reached in the lands of the world, with its variation. When the exception was made from it of those who believed and did righteous deeds, the ruling remained established for those other than the believers, as will come.

Al-khusr (loss) is a verbal noun, and it is the opposite of profit in trade. It is borrowed here for bad outcome for one who thinks a good outcome is for himself, and that is the lasting outcome, which is the outcome of man in his Hereafter, of bliss or punishment.

It was previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿So their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] in surah al-Baqarah. And its counterparts recur in the Qur'an, near and far.

The adverbial form (zarfiyya) in His saying: ﴿indeed, in loss﴾ is figurative: it likened the constant attachment of loss to the encompassing of the container by the contained, so it was more eloquent than saying: "Indeed, man is a loser."

The coming of this report in generality, with its emphasis by the oath and the emphatic particle in its answer, conveys awe and warning regarding the condition that encompasses most people.

It was followed by the exception in His saying: ﴿except those who have believed﴾ and so on. Thus the ruling becomes fully established in the hearer's mind, clarifying that people are of two groups: a group to whom loss reaches, and a group to whom none of it reaches. Those who believed and did righteous deeds, loss does not reach them in any way, provided they do not leave any of the righteous deeds by committing their opposites, which are the evil deeds.

Among the greatest righteous deeds is repentance from sins for those who commit them. Whoever has the attribute of faith realized in him and did not do evil deeds, or did them and repented of them, then the opposite of loss is realized for him, which is figurative profit, that is, the goodness of the outcome of his affair. As for whoever did not do righteous deeds and did not repent of his evil deeds, the ruling of the excepted-from is realized in him, which is loss.

This loss varies. The greatest and most enduring of it is the loss resulting from the absence of faith in God's oneness and the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ). Beyond that, the degrees of loss vary according to the abundance of evil deeds, outward and inward. And what Islam has set as degrees of deeds

[Page 534]

The Almighty's saying ﴿and they enjoined one another to the truth, and they enjoined one another to patience﴾ encompasses the establishing of all the religious interests. Thus the Islamic creeds and the religious ethics are included in the truth, and righteous deeds and avoiding evil deeds are included in patience.

Cultivating patience is the foundation of all the virtues of character, for training oneself in praiseworthy character necessarily involves a person compelling himself to oppose many desires. Opposing them involves hardship, which requires patience in bearing it, until noble character becomes a settled disposition (malakah) for the one who has trained his soul in it. As 'Amr ibn al-'As said:

*"When a man does not leave a food he loves,*
*and does not restrain a deluded heart wherever it wanders,*
*he will soon find for himself, through all time, a disgrace,*
*whose like, when mentioned, fills the mouths."*

[Page 534 continued]

Likewise, all righteous deeds involve compelling the soul to abandon what it inclines toward. In a hadith: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires." And from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Patience is a mount that does not stumble."

The discussion of patience has already been treated at length at the Almighty's saying ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:45] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The form of the verb "enjoining one another" with the truth and with patience indicates that the condition of believers' lives is to be founded on the widespread mutual exhortation to these two as a constant habit. This requires that believers be characterized by upholding the truth and by patience with what is disliked in the interests of Islam and its community. This accords with the customary understanding of people: no one enjoins another to constantly maintain a matter unless he himself regards that matter as deserving of constancy, since it is rare for anyone to undertake a matter of truth that he does not himself practice, or to urge patience while being impatient himself. The Almighty has said, rebuking the Children of Israel: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book? Will you not reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:44]. This meaning was also mentioned earlier at the Almighty's saying ﴿and do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾ [al-Fajr 89:18] in Surah al-Fajr.

Surah al-Humazah

This surah is named in the mushaf and in most tafsir works "Surat al-Humazah" with the definite article. In Sahih al-Bukhari and some tafsir works it is titled "Surat Wayl li-kulli humazah." Al-Fayruzabadi, in Basa'ir dhawi al-tamyiz, mentions that it is also called "Surat al-Hutamah" because this word occurs in it.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the thirty-second in the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Qiyamah and before Surat al-Mursalat.

Its verses number nine by consensus.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning a group of polytheists who had set themselves up to revile and insult the Muslims and to fabricate evil reports about them. Among these polytheists named were al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Jamil ibn Ma'mar of Banu Jumah (this man embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest and was present at Hunayn), and al-'As ibn Wa'il of Banu Sahm. All of them were among the chiefs of Quraysh. Also named were al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth and al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafiyyan, chiefs of the Thaqif from the people of al-Ta'if. All of these were people of wealth in the pre-Islamic period, flourishing through their riches and nobility. The verses of the surah came in general terms, so its ruling encompassed those named and whoever was of their kind among the polytheists, and their names were not mentioned.

* * *

The purpose of this surah is a warning to a group of polytheists who made defaming and slandering the Muslims a form of harm to them, hoping that the weariness of these kinds of harm would drive them to turn away from Islam and return to polytheism.
